title: Ἶρις καὶ Τρῶες
titleEn: Iris and the Trojan Host — Iliad 2.780–877
about: The Achaean army moves out, and the earth groans beneath it as it groans under Zeus when he lashes the ground around Typhoeus. Iris comes from Zeus to the Trojans, who are in assembly at Priam’s doors, takes the voice of the scout Polites, and tells the old man that she has never seen so great an army; she charges Hector to have each ally lead out his own countrymen, since the allies speak many tongues. Hector breaks up the assembly, the gates open, and the army pours out to a hill in front of the city, where the Trojans and their allies are sorted. The Catalogue of the Trojans then goes through the contingents with their leaders, from Hector, Aeneas and Pandarus to Sarpedon and Glaucus of Lycia, and on the way the poet looks ahead to two of the allies, who will die at the hands of Achilles in a river.

sentences.t: οἳ δ’ ἄρ’ ἴσαν ὡς εἴ τε πυρὶ χθὼν πᾶσα νέμοιτο·
sentences.l: And they then went as if by fire all the earth were being fed upon;
sentences.i: On they went, as if all the earth were being consumed by fire;
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ ‘and they’ has no noun: it is the army whose ships the Catalogue has just listed, now moving out. ἴσαν is the imperfect of εἶμι ‘go’ (Attic ᾔεσαν). ὡς εἴ τε is ‘as if’ and takes the optative νέμοιτο; νέμομαι, which in this part is ‘inhabit’ of men, is said of fire ‘feed on, spread over’, and πυρί is the dative of the fire doing it, so ‘all the earth were being fed upon by fire’. χθών ‘earth’ is a poetic word.

sentences.t:
γαῖα δ’ ὑπεστενάχιζε Διὶ ὣς τερπικεραύνῳ
χωομένῳ ὅτε τ’ ἀμφὶ Τυφωέϊ γαῖαν ἱμάσσῃ
εἰν Ἀρίμοις, ὅθι φασὶ Τυφωέος ἔμμεναι εὐνάς·
sentences.i: and the earth groaned beneath them as it groans under Zeus, who delights in the thunderbolt, when he is incensed and lashes the earth about Typhoeus, among the Arimi, where they say Typhoeus has his bed;
sentences.n: The comparison is with Zeus’s anger. γαῖα δ’ ‘and the earth’ is the subject of ὑπεστενάχιζε ‘groaned beneath’ (ὑπο- + στεναχίζω). Διὶ … χωομένῳ is ‘under Zeus, incensed’, with ὣς ‘as’ standing after the noun it goes with (= ὡς Διί); τερπικεραύνῳ ‘who delights in the thunderbolt’ is his stock epithet. ὅτε τ’ … ἱμάσσῃ ‘whenever he lashes’ is an aorist subjunctive in a general statement, and ἀμφὶ Τυφωέϊ ‘about Typhoeus’ says whom the blows fall around. εἰν is ἐν. Ἀρίμοις ‘among the Arimi’ is a name in the dative; whether it is a people or a place, and where, is not known. φασί ‘they say’ keeps the story at a distance, and εὐνάς ‘beds’ is a plural for the one lair.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρα τῶν ὑπὸ ποσσὶ μέγα στεναχίζετο γαῖα
ἐρχομένων·
sentences.l:
So then under the feet of them greatly groaned the earth
as they went;
sentences.i: So the earth groaned loudly beneath their feet as they went on;
sentences.n: ὣς ἄρα ‘so then’ closes the comparison: what the earth does under Zeus it did now under the marching men. τῶν ‘of them’ is the pronoun (the article as a pronoun) and depends on ποσσί, the epic dative plural of πούς: ὑπὸ ποσσί ‘under the feet’. στεναχίζετο is the imperfect middle of στεναχίζω ‘groan’, with a passive-looking ending but an active sense, and μέγα, the neuter of μέγας, is an adverb, ‘greatly, loudly’. ἐρχομένων is the genitive participle of ἔρχομαι ‘go’, agreeing with τῶν. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of 785.

sentences.t: μάλα δ’ ὦκα διέπρησσον πεδίοιο.
sentences.l: and very quickly they were crossing the plain.
sentences.i: and they were crossing the plain very quickly.
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of 785. μάλα δ’ ὦκα is ‘and very quickly’, ὦκα being the adverb of ὠκύς ‘swift’. διέπρησσον is the imperfect of διαπρήσσω ‘get through, accomplish’, here ‘cross’, with the genitive πεδίοιο (epic -οιο, = -ου) ‘across the plain’, a genitive of the ground covered.

sentences.t:
Τρωσὶν δ’ ἄγγελος ἦλθε ποδήνεμος ὠκέα Ἶρις
πὰρ Διὸς αἰγιόχοιο σὺν ἀγγελίῃ ἀλεγεινῇ·
sentences.l:
And to the Trojans a messenger came, wind-footed, swift Iris,
from beside aegis-bearing Zeus, with grievous news;
sentences.i: Iris, wind-footed and swift, came to the Trojans as a messenger from aegis-bearing Zeus, with grievous news;
sentences.n: A new paragraph and a new scene: the Trojans, not the Achaeans. Τρωσίν is the dative plural of Τρώς ‘Trojan’ (nominative plural Τρῶες), ‘to the Trojans’. ἄγγελος ‘messenger’ stands in apposition to Ἶρις ‘Iris’. ποδήνεμος ‘wind-footed’ is built on πούς ‘foot’ and ἄνεμος ‘wind’, and ὠκέα is the feminine of ὠκύς ‘swift’. πὰρ is παρά with the genitive, ‘from beside’, and Διὸς αἰγιόχοιο is the stock ‘aegis-bearing Zeus’ (epic genitive -οιο). ἀγγελίῃ ‘news’ and ἀλεγεινῇ ‘grievous’ agree, in the dative after σύν ‘with’.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἀγορὰς ἀγόρευον ἐπὶ Πριάμοιο θύρῃσι
πάντες ὁμηγερέες ἠμὲν νέοι ἠδὲ γέροντες·
sentences.l:
and they were holding assemblies at the doors of Priam,
all gathered together, both young and old;
sentences.i: and they were meeting in assembly at Priam’s doors, all gathered together, young men and old alike;
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ ‘and they’ are the Trojans, as the dative Τρωσίν in 786 shows. ἀγορὰς ἀγόρευον is a verb with its own noun, ‘were speaking assemblies’, that is ‘were holding assembly’: ἀγορεύω is ‘speak in assembly’ and ἀγορά (epic ἀγορή) ‘assembly’. θύρῃσι is the epic dative plural of θύρη ‘door’, so they sit at Priam’s doors. ὁμηγερέες ‘gathered together’ agrees with πάντες ‘all’, and ἠμὲν … ἠδέ is ‘both … and’, joining νέοι ‘young’ and γέροντες ‘old men’.

sentences.t: ἀγχοῦ δ’ ἱσταμένη προσέφη πόδας ὠκέα Ἶρις·
sentences.l: And standing close by, swift-in-feet Iris spoke;
sentences.i: Iris, swift of foot, came and stood close by, and spoke;
sentences.n: ἀγχοῦ ‘close by’ and ἱσταμένη ‘standing’ (the feminine participle of ἵσταμαι) belong to Iris, who has come down among the Trojans. προσέφη is the past tense of πρόσφημι ‘speak to’; it needs a person spoken to, who is not named here, since the Greek stops to say what shape she took (791–794) and the speech itself begins only at 796. πόδας ὠκέα Ἶρις ‘Iris, swift of foot’ is the stock formula, with πόδας an accusative of respect (‘swift in respect of feet’) and ὠκέα the feminine of ὠκύς.

sentences.t:
εἴσατο δὲ φθογγὴν υἷϊ Πριάμοιο Πολίτῃ,
ὃς Τρώων σκοπὸς ἷζε ποδωκείῃσι πεποιθὼς
τύμβῳ ἐπ’ ἀκροτάτῳ Αἰσυήταο γέροντος,
δέγμενος ὁππότε ναῦφιν ἀφορμηθεῖεν Ἀχαιοί·
sentences.l:
and she made herself like in voice to the son of Priam, Polites,
who as lookout of the Trojans sat, trusting in his fleet-footedness,
on the topmost tomb of Aesyetes the old man,
waiting for when from the ships should set out the Achaeans;
sentences.i: and she made herself like the son of Priam, Polites, in voice, who sat as a lookout for the Trojans, trusting in his speed of foot, on the very top of the tomb of old Aesyetes, waiting for the moment when the Achaeans should set out from the ships;
sentences.n: Iris disguises herself as a Trojan scout. εἴσατο is the aorist middle of εἴδομαι ‘make oneself like’, with φθογγήν, an accusative of respect, ‘in voice’, and the dative υἷϊ Πριάμοιο Πολίτῃ ‘to the son of Priam, Polites’. ὃς … ἷζε is ‘who sat’ (ἷζε intransitive here) and σκοπός ‘lookout’. ποδωκείῃσι is an abstract noun in the epic dative plural, ‘fleetness of foot’, from ποδώκης ‘fleet-footed’, with πεποιθώς, the perfect participle of πείθομαι, ‘trusting in’. τύμβῳ ἐπ’ ἀκροτάτῳ is ‘on the topmost tomb’, ἀκροτάτῳ being the superlative of ἄκρος ‘top’ and the tomb that of old Aesyetes (Αἰσυήταο, epic genitive -αο). δέγμενος is an old short aorist participle of δέχομαι, ‘waiting for’; ὁππότε … ἀφορμηθεῖεν ‘for the time when … should set out’ is an optative for an event expected in the future, and ναῦφιν has the old ending -φιν, ‘from the ships’.

sentences.t: τῷ μιν ἐεισαμένη προσέφη πόδας ὠκέα Ἶρις·
sentences.l: Having made herself like to him, addressed him swift-in-feet Iris:
sentences.i: Making herself like Polites, Iris, swift of foot, said to the old man:
sentences.n: τῷ ‘to him’ is Polites and goes with ἐεισαμένη, the aorist participle of εἴδομαι (the verb of εἴσατο, 791) ‘having made herself like’. μιν ‘him’ is a different man: the one she speaks to, whom the Greek does not name here. The English says ‘the old man’ because the next line opens with the vocative ὦ γέρον ‘old man’, and because ‘him’ would read as Polites. The formula πόδας ὠκέα Ἶρις is the one of 790.

sentences.t:
ὦ γέρον αἰεί τοι μῦθοι φίλοι ἄκριτοί εἰσιν,
ὥς ποτ’ ἐπ’ εἰρήνης·
sentences.l:
“Old man, always to you words are dear, unsorted,
as once in peace;
sentences.i: “Old man, endless talk is always dear to you, as it was once in time of peace;
sentences.n: Iris’s speech begins with ὦ γέρον ‘old man’, said to the old man of 795. τοι is σοι ‘to you’, φίλοι ‘dear’, and ἄκριτοι ‘unsorted’ (ἀ- + κρίνω ‘sort, decide’) says of μῦθοι ‘words’ that they never reach a decision, so ‘endless’. εἰσιν is ‘are’. ὥς ποτ’ ἐπ’ εἰρήνης is ‘as once in peace’, with ἐπί and the genitive meaning ‘in the time of’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of 797.

sentences.t: πόλεμος δ’ ἀλίαστος ὄρωρεν.
sentences.l: but war, relentless, has arisen.
sentences.i: but a relentless war has arisen.
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of 797. πόλεμος δ’ ‘but war’ sets the present against the peace just named. ἀλίαστος is rare and its origin is not certain (perhaps ἀ- + λιάζομαι ‘give way’), with the sense ‘unyielding, relentless’. ὄρωρεν is the perfect of ὄρνυμι ‘stir up’, used intransitively, ‘has risen, is on foot’.

sentences.t:
ἤδη μὲν μάλα πολλὰ μάχας εἰσήλυθον ἀνδρῶν,
ἀλλ’ οὔ πω τοιόνδε τοσόνδέ τε λαὸν ὄπωπα·
sentences.l:
Already very many times into the battles of men I have gone,
but never yet such and so great a people have I seen;
sentences.i: Many a time already I have gone into the battles of men, but never yet have I seen such an army, and one so great;
sentences.n: ἤδη μὲν … ἀλλ’ οὔ πω is ‘already, indeed … but never yet’. μάλα πολλά is a neuter plural used as an adverb, ‘very many times’, and μάχας … ἀνδρῶν ‘battles of men’ is the object of εἰσήλυθον, the epic aorist of εἰσέρχομαι ‘go into’ (Attic εἰσῆλθον). τοιόνδε τοσόνδε ‘of such a sort, and so great’ both describe λαόν, ‘people, army’, and ὄπωπα is the perfect of ὁράω, ‘have seen’. Iris is speaking as the scout Polites.

sentences.t:
λίην γὰρ φύλλοισιν ἐοικότες ἢ ψαμάθοισιν
ἔρχονται πεδίοιο μαχησόμενοι προτὶ ἄστυ.
sentences.l:
for exceedingly like leaves or sands
they come over the plain to fight toward the town.
sentences.i: for they are very like leaves or sands as they come over the plain to fight toward the town.
sentences.n: λίην ‘exceedingly’ goes with ἐοικότες, the perfect participle of ἔοικα ‘be like’, taking the datives φύλλοισιν ‘leaves’ and ψαμάθοισιν ‘sands’ (-οισιν, the epic dative plural). The point of the comparison is their number, which the Greek leaves unsaid. ἔρχονται ‘they come’, πεδίοιο ‘over the plain’ (a genitive of the ground crossed, as at 785), μαχησόμενοι ‘to fight’ (a future participle of purpose), προτὶ ἄστυ = πρὸς ἄστυ ‘toward the town’. ἄστυ is Troy, as 803 shows.

sentences.t: Ἕκτορ σοὶ δὲ μάλιστ’ ἐπιτέλλομαι, ὧδε δὲ ῥέξαι·
sentences.l: Hector, to you moreover most of all I enjoin, and thus to do:
sentences.i: Hector, to you above all I give this charge, and it is to act as follows:
sentences.n: Iris now turns from the old man to Hector: Ἕκτορ is the vocative. σοὶ δέ ‘and to you’ goes with μάλιστα ‘most of all’. ἐπιτέλλομαι is ‘I enjoin, I lay a charge’, the middle, taking a dative of the person and an infinitive, and ὧδε ‘thus’ with the aorist infinitive ῥέξαι of ῥέζω ‘do’ says what the charge is, the infinitive standing for an order.

sentences.t:
πολλοὶ γὰρ κατὰ ἄστυ μέγα Πριάμου ἐπίκουροι,
ἄλλη δ’ ἄλλων γλῶσσα πολυσπερέων ἀνθρώπων·
sentences.l:
For many through the great town of Priam are allies,
and different of different men is the tongue, of widely scattered men;
sentences.i: For there are many allies throughout the great town of Priam, and there is a different tongue for each of these widely scattered men;
sentences.n: πολλοὶ … ἐπίκουροι ‘many allies’ has no verb, and ‘are’ is understood. ἐπίκουρος is a helper from elsewhere, an ally. κατὰ ἄστυ is ‘throughout the town’. ἄλλη δ’ ἄλλων γλῶσσα is ‘and different is the tongue of different men’: ἄλλη (feminine singular, agreeing with γλῶσσα ‘tongue’) is set against ἄλλων (genitive plural). πολυσπερέων ‘widely scattered’ (πολύς + σπείρω ‘sow, scatter’; epic genitive plural -έων) agrees with ἀνθρώπων. This is why the allies must be sorted by their own leaders, as the next lines say.

sentences.t:
τοῖσιν ἕκαστος ἀνὴρ σημαινέτω οἷσί περ ἄρχει,
τῶν δ’ ἐξηγείσθω κοσμησάμενος πολιήτας.
sentences.l:
To them let each man give orders, to those whom he leads,
and of these let him lead out, having marshalled the citizens.”
sentences.i: let each man give orders to those he leads, and lead them out once he has marshalled his fellow-citizens.”
sentences.n: τοῖσιν ‘to them’ (the allies, epic dative plural) and οἷσί περ ἄρχει ‘to whom he is leader’ (ἄρχω ‘lead’ with the dative) frame σημαινέτω, the third-person imperative of σημαίνω ‘give orders, give the word’. ἕκαστος ἀνήρ ‘each man’ is the leader of each contingent. τῶν δ’ ἐξηγείσθω is ‘and of these let him lead the way’, ἐξηγέομαι taking the genitive of those led, and κοσμησάμενος, the aorist participle of κοσμέω ‘set in order, marshal’, has the object πολιήτας ‘citizens’ (accusative plural of πολιήτης, a man of one city). The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφαθ’, Ἕκτωρ δ’ οὔ τι θεᾶς ἔπος ἠγνοίησεν,
αἶψα δ’ ἔλυσ’ ἀγορήν·
sentences.l:
So she spoke, and Hector did not at all fail to recognize the goddess’s word,
and quickly he loosed the assembly;
sentences.i: So she spoke, and Hector did not fail at all to know the goddess’s word, and quickly broke up the assembly;
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφαθ’ ‘so she spoke’ ends Iris’s speech (ἔφαθ’ is ἔφατο, elided, the τ becoming θ before the rough breathing of Ἕκτωρ). οὔ τι … ἠγνοίησεν is a double negative: ἀγνοιέω is ‘fail to know’, so with οὔ τι ‘not at all’ it says that Hector knew the goddess’s word for what it was; θεᾶς ἔπος is ‘the goddess’s word’. αἶψα ‘quickly’; ἔλυσ’ is ἔλυσε, elided, from λύω ‘loose, release’, with ἀγορήν ‘assembly’ (epic ἀγορή = Attic ἀγορά), so he dissolved the assembly. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of 808.

sentences.t: ἐπὶ τεύχεα δ’ ἐσσεύοντο·
sentences.l: and for armour they rushed;
sentences.i: and they rushed for their armour;
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of 808. ἐπὶ τεύχεα is ‘for the armour’, with ἐπί of the thing aimed at; τεύχεα is the neuter plural in -εα (Attic τεύχη). The subject, the Trojans and their allies, is not named. ἐσσεύοντο is the imperfect middle of σεύω ‘set in motion’, here ‘rushed’, with the σ doubled.

sentences.t:
πᾶσαι δ’ ὠΐγνυντο πύλαι, ἐκ δ’ ἔσσυτο λαὸς
πεζοί θ’ ἱππῆές τε·
sentences.l:
and all the gates were being opened, and out rushed the people,
both on foot and horsemen;
sentences.i: all the gates were opened, and out rushed the army, both on foot and mounted;
sentences.n: πύλαι ‘gates’ is plural, with πᾶσαι ‘all’; ὠΐγνυντο is the imperfect passive of οἴγνυμι ‘open’. ἐκ … ἔσσυτο is ‘rushed out’, ἔσσυτο being the aorist of σεύομαι (the root of ἐσσεύοντο, 808) with ἐκ standing apart from it (tmesis); λαός ‘people, army’ is singular and takes a singular verb. πεζοί θ’ ἱππῆές τε is ‘both on foot and horsemen’: πεζοί ‘men on foot’ and ἱππῆες ‘horsemen’ (the epic form of ἱππεῖς). The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of 810.

sentences.t: πολὺς δ’ ὀρυμαγδὸς ὀρώρει.
sentences.l: and a great din had risen.
sentences.i: and a great din rose.
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of 810. πολὺς … ὀρυμαγδός is ‘a great din’, a noise of many sounds together. ὀρώρει is the pluperfect of ὄρνυμι (the verb of ὄρωρεν, 797), ‘had sprung up’, which in English reads as a plain past, ‘went up’.

sentences.t:
ἔστι δέ τις προπάροιθε πόλιος αἰπεῖα κολώνη
ἐν πεδίῳ ἀπάνευθε περίδρομος ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα,
τὴν ἤτοι ἄνδρες Βατίειαν κικλήσκουσιν,
ἀθάνατοι δέ τε σῆμα πολυσκάρθμοιο Μυρίνης·
sentences.l:
Now there is a certain steep hill before the city
in the plain, apart, that can be run round on this side and on that,
which indeed men call Batieia,
but the immortals the tomb of much-leaping Myrine;
sentences.i: Now there is a steep hill in front of the city, out in the plain and standing apart, with room to run round it on this side and on that, which men call Batieia, but the immortals call the tomb of the much-leaping Myrine;
sentences.n: A new paragraph, and the place where the army is drawn up. ἔστι … τις is ‘there is a certain’; προπάροιθε πόλιος is ‘in front of the city’ (πόλιος, epic genitive of πόλις); αἰπεῖα is the feminine of αἰπύς ‘steep’, and κολώνη is ‘hill’. περίδρομος ‘running round’ says that it stands clear, so that one can run round it ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα ‘on this side and on that’. τὴν ἤτοι … κικλήσκουσιν is ‘which men indeed call’ (ἤτοι is printed as one word), with Βατίειαν ‘Batieia’ the name men use; ἀθάνατοι δέ τε ‘but the immortals’ gives the gods’ name, and ‘call it’ is understood from the verb before. σῆμα ‘tomb’ (a mark set over a grave) belongs to Μυρίνης ‘Myrine’, whom the Greek does not describe; πολυσκάρθμοιο ‘much-leaping’ is built on πολύς and σκαρθμός ‘leap’. Line 814 is metrically irregular as transmitted, at the name Μυρίνης: it scans only if its υ is counted short.

sentences.t: ἔνθα τότε Τρῶές τε διέκριθεν ἠδ’ ἐπίκουροι.
sentences.l: There then were parted both the Trojans and the allies.
sentences.i: There, then, the Trojans and the allies were parted.
sentences.n: ἔνθα τότε is ‘there, then’, at the hill. διέκριθεν is the aorist passive of διακρίνω ‘part, separate’, with the epic ending -θεν for -θησαν, so ‘were parted’: the Trojans from their allies, and then each people from the next, as the lines that follow go through them one by one. ἐπίκουροι ‘allies’ is as at 803.

sentences.t:
Τρωσὶ μὲν ἡγεμόνευε μέγας κορυθαίολος Ἕκτωρ
Πριαμίδης·
sentences.l:
Of the Trojans indeed was leader great Hector of the glancing helmet,
Priam’s-son;
sentences.i: Great Hector of the glancing helmet, son of Priam, was the leader of the Trojans;
sentences.n: Τρωσί is a dative of the people led, ‘of the Trojans’, with ἡγεμόνευε ‘was leader’ (ἡγεμονεύω), and μέν marks this as the first entry of the list. μέγας ‘great’ and κορυθαίολος ‘of the glancing helmet’ (κόρυς ‘helmet’ + αἰόλος ‘quick-moving, glancing’) are Hector’s stock epithets; Πριαμίδης is the patronymic, ‘son of Priam’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of 817.

sentences.t:
ἅμα τῷ γε πολὺ πλεῖστοι καὶ ἄριστοι
λαοὶ θωρήσσοντο μεμαότες ἐγχείῃσι.
sentences.l:
with him by far the most numerous and the best
people armed themselves, eager with spears.
sentences.i: By far the most numerous and the best of the troops armed themselves with him, eager with their spears.
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of 817. ἅμα τῷ γε is ‘together with him’ (ἅμα with the dative; τῷ is the pronoun, Hector). πολὺ πλεῖστοι καὶ ἄριστοι is ‘by far the most numerous and the best’: πολύ is the adverb ‘by far’, with two superlatives, and the noun they describe, λαοί ‘people, troops’, comes in the next line. θωρήσσοντο is the imperfect middle of θωρήσσω ‘arm’, and μεμαότες, the perfect participle of μέμονα ‘be eager’, goes with ἐγχείῃσι, the epic dative plural of ἐγχείη ‘spear’: ‘eager with their spears’, the dative saying where the eagerness is bent.

sentences.t:
Δαρδανίων αὖτ’ ἦρχεν ἐῢς πάϊς Ἀγχίσαο
Αἰνείας, τὸν ὑπ’ Ἀγχίσῃ τέκε δῖ’ Ἀφροδίτη
Ἴδης ἐν κνημοῖσι θεὰ βροτῷ εὐνηθεῖσα,
sentences.l:
Of the Dardanians, in turn, was leading the good son of Anchises,
Aeneas, whom to Anchises bore heavenly Aphrodite
in the spurs of Ida, a goddess having lain with a mortal,
sentences.i: Of the Dardanians, in turn, led the good son of Anchises, Aeneas, whom heavenly Aphrodite bore to Anchises in the spurs of Ida, a goddess who had lain with a mortal,
sentences.n: Δαρδανίων αὖτ’ ἦρχεν is ‘of the Dardanians, in turn, led’ (αὖτ’ = αὖτε), ἄρχω taking the genitive of the people led. ἐῢς is the epic form of ἐΰς ‘good’, and πάϊς (= παῖς) with Ἀγχίσαο, the epic genitive of Ἀγχίσης, is ‘son of Anchises’; he is Αἰνείας, Aeneas. τὸν … τέκε is ‘whom she bore’ (unaugmented), and ὑπ’ Ἀγχίσῃ ‘to Anchises’ names the father (with τίκτω, ὑπό and the dative do this). δῖα Ἀφροδίτη is ‘heavenly Aphrodite’, δῖος being the stock ‘heavenly’. Ἴδης ἐν κνημοῖσι is ‘in the spurs of Ida’, κνημός being the shoulder of a mountain. θεά ‘a goddess’ stands in apposition to Aphrodite, βροτῷ ‘with a mortal’ is a dative, and εὐνηθεῖσα is the aorist passive participle of εὐνάζω ‘put to bed’, here ‘having lain with’. Line 819 is metrically irregular as transmitted: its fifth foot is a spondee, and the short α of the ending of Ἀγχίσαο has to count long.

sentences.t:
οὐκ οἶος, ἅμα τῷ γε δύω Ἀντήνορος υἷε
Ἀρχέλοχός τ’ Ἀκάμας τε μάχης εὖ εἰδότε πάσης.
sentences.l:
not alone: with him the two sons of Antenor,
Archelochus and Acamas, both knowing all fighting well.
sentences.i: He did not lead alone: with him were the two sons of Antenor, Archelochus and Acamas, who both knew all fighting well.
sentences.n: οὐκ οἶος ‘not alone’ has no verb of its own; the leading of 819 is carried over. ἅμα τῷ γε is ‘together with him’, as at 817. δύω … υἷε are duals, ‘two sons’, of Ἀντήνορος (genitive of Ἀντήνωρ), and the two are Ἀρχέλοχος and Ἀκάμας. εἰδότε is the dual perfect participle of οἶδα ‘know’, ‘both knowing’, with εὖ ‘well’ and the genitive μάχης … πάσης ‘all fighting’.

sentences.t:
οἳ δὲ Ζέλειαν ἔναιον ὑπαὶ πόδα νείατον Ἴδης
ἀφνειοὶ πίνοντες ὕδωρ μέλαν Αἰσήποιο
Τρῶες, τῶν αὖτ’ ἦρχε Λυκάονος ἀγλαὸς υἱὸς
Πάνδαρος, ᾧ καὶ τόξον Ἀπόλλων αὐτὸς ἔδωκεν.
sentences.l:
And they who in Zeleia dwelt beneath the lowest foot of Ida,
rich, drinking the dark water of the Aesepus,
Trojans, of these in turn was leading Lycaon’s splendid son
Pandarus, to whom even the bow Apollo himself gave.
sentences.i: And those who dwelt in Zeleia, beneath the lowest foot of Ida, rich men who drank the dark water of the Aesepus, Trojans, were led in turn by Lycaon’s splendid son Pandarus, to whom Apollo himself had given even the bow.
sentences.n: οἳ δὲ … ἔναιον opens a new entry, ‘and those who dwelt in’, the imperfect of ναίω; Ζέλειαν is the town Zeleia. ὑπαί is ὑπό in its epic form, and πόδα νείατον Ἴδης is ‘the lowest foot of Ida’, the base of the mountain, νείατον being a superlative ‘lowest’. ἀφνειοί ‘rich’, πίνοντες ‘drinking’, μέλαν ὕδωρ ‘dark water’, Αἰσήποιο ‘of the Aesepus’ (epic genitive). Τρῶες ‘Trojans’ stands in apposition to οἳ. τῶν αὖτ’ ἦρχε is ‘of these, in turn, led’. Λυκάονος ἀγλαὸς υἱός is ‘Lycaon’s splendid son’, Pandarus. ᾧ is the relative in the dative, ‘to whom’, and καί ‘even’ goes with τόξον ‘the bow’: the god gave him the bow itself.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ Ἀδρήστειάν τ’ εἶχον καὶ δῆμον Ἀπαισοῦ
καὶ Πιτύειαν ἔχον καὶ Τηρείης ὄρος αἰπύ,
τῶν ἦρχ’ Ἄδρηστός τε καὶ Ἄμφιος λινοθώρηξ
υἷε δύω Μέροπος Περκωσίου,
sentences.l:
And those who held Adrasteia and the land of Apaesus
and held Pityeia and the steep mountain of Tereia,
of these were leading Adrastus and Amphius, linen-breastplated,
the two sons of Merops of Percote,
sentences.i: And those who held Adrasteia and the land of Apaesus, and held Pityeia and the steep mountain of Tereia, of these Adrastus and Amphius, who wore a linen breastplate, led, the two sons of Merops of Percote,
sentences.n: A new entry: οἳ δ’ … εἶχον … ἔχον is ‘and those who held … and held’ (ἔχον is the unaugmented imperfect), with four places: Ἀδρήστειαν ‘Adrasteia’, δῆμον Ἀπαισοῦ ‘the land of Apaesus’ (δῆμος is a place here, not a people), Πιτύειαν ‘Pityeia’, and Τηρείης ὄρος αἰπύ ‘the steep mountain of Tereia’. τῶν ἦρχ’ is ‘of these led’, with ἦρχ’ (ἦρχε, singular) before the two names, Ἄδρηστος (the Ionic form of Ἄδραστος) and Ἄμφιος. λινοθώρηξ ‘wearing a linen breastplate’ goes with Ἄμφιος, and υἷε δύω ‘the two sons’ is dual, of Μέροπος Περκωσίου ‘Merops of Percote’, Περκώσιος being the adjective from the town Percote, named at 835. The long sentence is cut at this comma.

sentences.t:
ὃς περὶ πάντων
ᾔδεε μαντοσύνας, οὐδὲ οὓς παῖδας ἔασκε
στείχειν ἐς πόλεμον φθισήνορα·
sentences.i: who knew the arts of prophecy beyond all others, and would not allow his own sons to go to the war that wastes men;
sentences.n: ὃς is Merops. περὶ πάντων is ‘beyond all (others)’, with ᾔδεε, the epic uncontracted pluperfect of οἶδα, ‘he knew’ (Attic ᾔδει), and μαντοσύνας ‘arts of prophecy, seercraft’. οὓς … παῖδας is ‘his own sons’ (ὅς is the possessive here, not the relative), ἔασκε is the iterative of ἐάω ‘allow’ (-σκ- marks a repeated or habitual act, ‘he would not allow’), and στείχειν is ‘to go’. φθισήνορα, built on φθίω ‘waste’ and ἀνήρ ‘man’, is the epithet of war, ‘that wastes men’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of 833.

sentences.t:
τὼ δέ οἱ οὔ τι
πειθέσθην·
sentences.l:
but those two to him not at all
obeyed;
sentences.i: but the two of them did not obey him at all;
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of 833. τὼ is the dual pronoun ‘those two’, the sons; οἱ is ‘to him’; οὔ τι ‘not at all’. πειθέσθην is the dual imperfect of πείθομαι ‘obey’, which takes the dative. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of 834.

sentences.t: κῆρες γὰρ ἄγον μέλανος θανάτοιο.
sentences.l: for the death-spirits of black death were bringing them on.
sentences.i: for the spirits of black death were bringing them on.
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of 834. κῆρες is the plural of κήρ ‘death-spirit’, the powers that carry men off to death, not to be confused with the neuter κῆρ ‘heart’ of 851; μέλανος θανάτοιο is ‘of black death’. ἄγον is the unaugmented imperfect of ἄγω, ‘were bringing’, and the sons, whom the verb brings on, are not named again.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἄρα Περκώτην καὶ Πράκτιον ἀμφενέμοντο
καὶ Σηστὸν καὶ Ἄβυδον ἔχον καὶ δῖαν Ἀρίσβην,
τῶν αὖθ’ Ὑρτακίδης ἦρχ’ Ἄσιος ὄρχαμος ἀνδρῶν,
sentences.l:
And those who Percote and Practius inhabited round about,
and held Sestus and Abydus and heavenly Arisbe,
of these in turn Hyrtacus’-son was leading, Asius, chief of men,
sentences.i: And those who inhabited the country round Percote and Practius, and held Sestus, Abydus and heavenly Arisbe, of these, in turn, led Asius, son of Hyrtacus, chief of men,
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ ἄρα … ἀμφενέμοντο is ‘and those who inhabited round about’: ἀμφί + νέμομαι ‘inhabit’, with the places Περκώτην ‘Percote’ and Πράκτιον ‘Practius’ (a town or river; the form does not show which). ἔχον ‘held’ takes Σηστόν ‘Sestus’, Ἄβυδον ‘Abydus’ and δῖαν Ἀρίσβην ‘heavenly Arisbe’, δῖος being the stock ‘heavenly’, here said of a town. τῶν αὖθ’ … ἦρχ’ is ‘of these, in turn, led’ (αὖθ’ = αὖθι, a by-form of αὖτε). Ὑρτακίδης is a patronymic, ‘son of Hyrtacus’, and Ἄσιος ὄρχαμος ἀνδρῶν is ‘Asius, chief of men’, with the stock ὄρχαμος ἀνδρῶν.

sentences.t:
Ἄσιος Ὑρτακίδης ὃν Ἀρίσβηθεν φέρον ἵπποι
αἴθωνες μεγάλοι ποταμοῦ ἄπο Σελλήεντος.
sentences.l:
Asius, Hyrtacus’-son, whom from Arisbe were bearing horses,
fire-bright, big, from the river Selleis.
sentences.i: Asius, son of Hyrtacus, whom fire-bright and big horses carried from Arisbe, from the river Selleis.
sentences.n: The name and patronymic of the last line are said again, and the new clause tells how the man came. ὃν … φέρον is ‘whom … were carrying’ (φέρον, unaugmented imperfect of φέρω), ἵπποι is ‘horses’, and Ἀρίσβηθεν ‘from Arisbe’ has the ending -θεν, ‘from’. αἴθωνες is ‘burning, blazing’, taken here of the horses’ colour (the Greek does not say which), and μεγάλοι ‘big’. ποταμοῦ ἄπο Σελλήεντος is ‘from the river Selleis’, with ἄπο standing after its noun.

sentences.t:
Ἱππόθοος δ’ ἄγε φῦλα Πελασγῶν ἐγχεσιμώρων
τῶν οἳ Λάρισαν ἐριβώλακα ναιετάασκον·
sentences.l:
And Hippothous brought the tribes of the spear-wielding Pelasgians,
of those who rich-soiled Larissa kept dwelling in;
sentences.i: And Hippothous brought the tribes of the spear-wielding Pelasgians, those who dwelt in rich-soiled Larissa;
sentences.n: Ἱππόθοος is ‘Hippothous’, ἄγε ‘brought’ (unaugmented), φῦλα ‘tribes’ (the neuter plural of φῦλον), and Πελασγῶν ἐγχεσιμώρων ‘of the spear-wielding Pelasgians’, ἐγχεσίμωρος being a stock epithet. τῶν οἳ is ‘of those who’, taking a part of the Pelasgians; Λάρισαν ἐριβώλακα is ‘rich-soiled Larissa’ (ἐριβῶλαξ, accusative -ακα), and ναιετάασκον is the iterative of ναιετάω ‘dwell’ (‘used to dwell’; the -σκ- marks habit). The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
τῶν ἦρχ’ Ἱππόθοός τε Πύλαιός τ’ ὄζος Ἄρηος,
υἷε δύω Λήθοιο Πελασγοῦ Τευταμίδαο.
sentences.l:
Of these were leading Hippothous and Pylaeus, scion of Ares,
the two sons of Lethus the Pelasgian, Teutamus’-son.
sentences.i: Of these Hippothous and Pylaeus, scion of Ares, led, the two sons of Lethus the Pelasgian, son of Teutamus.
sentences.n: τῶν ἦρχ’ is ‘of these led’, with ἦρχ’ (ἦρχε, singular) before the two names Ἱππόθοος and Πύλαιος. ὄζος Ἄρηος ‘scion of Ares’ is singular, so grammatically it goes with Πύλαιος, the nearer name; ὄζος is literally ‘branch’, here an offshoot or descendant. υἷε δύω is dual, ‘the two sons’, of Λήθοιο (epic genitive of Λῆθος, Lethus). Πελασγοῦ ‘the Pelasgian’ agrees with Λήθοιο, and Τευταμίδαο is a patronymic with the epic ending -αο, ‘son of Teutamus’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Θρήϊκας ἦγ’ Ἀκάμας καὶ Πείροος ἥρως
ὅσσους Ἑλλήσποντος ἀγάρροος ἐντὸς ἐέργει.
sentences.l:
But the Thracians brought Acamas and the hero Peirous,
as many as the strong-flowing Hellespont shuts in within.
sentences.i: But Acamas and the hero Peirous brought the Thracians, as many as the strong-flowing Hellespont shuts in.
sentences.n: αὐτάρ ‘but’ begins the entry. Θρήϊκας ‘Thracians’ (the diaeresis shows that ηϊ is two sounds). ἦγ’ is ἦγε, ‘brought’, singular though two leaders follow, Ἀκάμας and Πείροος ἥρως ‘the hero Peirous’; Ἀκάμας is also the name of one of Antenor’s sons at 823, and nothing here links the two. ὅσσους … ἐντὸς ἐέργει is ‘as many as … shuts in within’, ἐέργει being the epic form of εἴργει ‘shut in, enclose’, and ἀγάρροος ‘strong-flowing’ is built on ἀγα- (an intensifier) and ῥόος ‘stream’. Ἑλλήσποντος is the Hellespont, the strait.

sentences.t:
Εὔφημος δ’ ἀρχὸς Κικόνων ἦν αἰχμητάων
υἱὸς Τροιζήνοιο διοτρεφέος Κεάδαο.
sentences.l:
And Euphemus was commander of the Cicones, spearmen,
son of Troezenus, Zeus-nurtured, Ceas’-son.
sentences.i: And Euphemus was commander of the Cicones, the spearmen, son of Troezenus, Zeus-nurtured, the son of Ceas.
sentences.n: Εὔφημος δ’ … ἦν ἀρχός is ‘and Euphemus was commander’, ἀρχός ‘commander’ taking the genitive Κικόνων ‘of the Cicones’, with αἰχμητάων ‘spearmen’, the epic genitive plural of αἰχμητής, as the stock description of a warrior people. υἱὸς Τροιζήνοιο is ‘son of Troezenus’; διοτρεφέος ‘Zeus-nurtured’ (epic genitive -έος) is his stock epithet. Κεάδαο has the ending -αο and is patronymic in form (compare Τευταμίδαο, 843), so it is taken as ‘son of Ceas’, a second description of Troezenus; the genitive could also be a name Ceades, and the Greek does not say.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Πυραίχμης ἄγε Παίονας ἀγκυλοτόξους
τηλόθεν ἐξ Ἀμυδῶνος ἀπ’ Ἀξιοῦ εὐρὺ ῥέοντος,
Ἀξιοῦ οὗ κάλλιστον ὕδωρ ἐπικίδναται αἶαν.
sentences.i: But Pyraechmes brought the Paeonians with their curved bows from far away, from Amydon, from the wide-flowing Axius, the Axius whose fairest water spreads over the land.
sentences.n: Πυραίχμης is ‘Pyraechmes’ and ἄγε ‘brought’ (unaugmented). ἀγκυλοτόξους is ‘of the curved bows’ (ἀγκύλος ‘curved’ + τόξον ‘bow’). τηλόθεν is ‘from far away’, ἐξ Ἀμυδῶνος ‘from Amydon’ (a town), and ἀπ’ Ἀξιοῦ ‘from the Axius’ (a river, the genitive after ἀπό); εὐρὺ ῥέοντος is ‘flowing wide’, εὐρύ being the adverb ‘widely’. The river’s name is said again at the start of the last line, where the relative Ἀξιοῦ οὗ ‘the Axius whose’ takes it up. ἐπικίδναται is the middle of ἐπικίδνημι, ‘spreads (itself) over’, and αἶαν ‘land’ is αἶα, a poetic word for γαῖα.

sentences.t:
Παφλαγόνων δ’ ἡγεῖτο Πυλαιμένεος λάσιον κῆρ
ἐξ Ἐνετῶν, ὅθεν ἡμιόνων γένος ἀγροτεράων,
sentences.l:
And of the Paphlagonians was leading the shaggy heart of Pylaemenes
from the Eneti, from where is the race of wild mules,
sentences.i: The shaggy heart of Pylaemenes led the Paphlagonians, from the Eneti, from where the race of wild mules comes,
sentences.n: Παφλαγόνων ‘of the Paphlagonians’ depends on ἡγεῖτο, the imperfect of ἡγέομαι ‘lead’. Πυλαιμένεος λάσιον κῆρ is ‘the shaggy heart of Pylaemenes’, which names the man by his heart; λάσιον ‘shaggy’ is said of a heart as στήθεσσιν λασίοισι ‘in his shaggy chest’ is said of a chest at 1.189, and κῆρ is the neuter ‘heart’, not κήρ ‘death-spirit’ (834). ἐξ Ἐνετῶν is ‘from the Eneti’, ὅθεν ‘from where’; γένος ἡμιόνων ἀγροτεράων is ‘the race of wild mules’, ἀγροτεράων being the epic genitive plural of ἀγρότερος ‘of the wild’.

sentences.t:
οἵ ῥα Κύτωρον ἔχον καὶ Σήσαμον ἀμφενέμοντο
ἀμφί τε Παρθένιον ποταμὸν κλυτὰ δώματ’ ἔναιον
Κρῶμνάν τ’ Αἰγιαλόν τε καὶ ὑψηλοὺς Ἐρυθίνους.
sentences.l:
who Cytorus held and Sesamus inhabited round about,
and about the river Parthenius famous halls dwelt in,
both Cromna and Aegialus and the high Erythini.
sentences.i: who held Cytorus and inhabited the country round Sesamus, and dwelt in famous halls about the river Parthenius, in Cromna, Aegialus and the high Erythini.
sentences.n: οἵ ῥα is ‘who, so’, the relative continuing the entry, with ῥα (= ἄρα) a light particle. ἔχον ‘held’, ἀμφενέμοντο ‘inhabited round about’ and ἔναιον ‘dwelt in’ are three different verbs for living in a place, kept apart in the English; Κύτωρον is ‘Cytorus’ and Σήσαμον ‘Sesamus’. ἀμφί τε Παρθένιον ποταμὸν is ‘and about the river Parthenius’, with κλυτὰ δώματ’ ἔναιον ‘dwelt in famous halls’, κλυτά being the stock ‘famous’. The last line adds three more places with ἔναιον: Κρῶμνάν ‘Cromna’, Αἰγιαλόν ‘Aegialus’ (a name, also the common word for a shore), and ὑψηλοὺς Ἐρυθίνους ‘the high Erythini’, a plural name.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ἁλιζώνων Ὀδίος καὶ Ἐπίστροφος ἦρχον
τηλόθεν ἐξ Ἀλύβης, ὅθεν ἀργύρου ἐστὶ γενέθλη.
sentences.l:
But of the Halizones Odius and Epistrophus were leading
from far away, from Alybe, from where is the origin of silver.
sentences.i: But Odius and Epistrophus led the Halizones from far away, from Alybe, where silver has its origin.
sentences.n: αὐτάρ ‘but’ begins the entry. Ἁλιζώνων ‘of the Halizones’ is a people, Ὀδίος ‘Odius’ and Ἐπίστροφος ‘Epistrophus’ the two leaders, and ἦρχον is plural, ‘were leading’. τηλόθεν is ‘from far away’, ἐξ Ἀλύβης ‘from Alybe’ (a place; the Greek does not say where), ὅθεν ‘from where’, and ἔστι … γενέθλη is ‘there is the origin’, γενέθλη (from the root of γίγνομαι) meaning ‘birth, origin’; ἀργύρου is ‘of silver’.

sentences.t: Μυσῶν δὲ Χρόμις ἦρχε καὶ Ἔννομος οἰωνιστής·
sentences.l: And of the Mysians Chromis was leading, and Ennomus the bird-diviner;
sentences.i: Chromis led the Mysians, and Ennomus, the reader of birds;
sentences.n: Μυσῶν ‘of the Mysians’ depends on ἦρχε ‘was leading’, which stands before the first name. Χρόμις is ‘Chromis’ and Ἔννομος ‘Ennomus’. οἰωνιστής ‘bird-diviner’ is built on οἰωνός ‘bird, bird of omen’ and is a man who reads the birds for signs, as οἰωνοπόλων does at 1.69. The ano teleia leads into the lines that say it did him no good.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ οὐκ οἰωνοῖσιν ἐρύσατο κῆρα μέλαιναν,
ἀλλ’ ἐδάμη ὑπὸ χερσὶ ποδώκεος Αἰακίδαο
ἐν ποταμῷ, ὅθι περ Τρῶας κεράϊζε καὶ ἄλλους.
sentences.l:
but not by birds did he draw off the black death-fate,
but he was subdued under the hands of the fleet-footed descendant of Aeacus
in the river, just where he was ravaging the Trojans and others.
sentences.i: But it was not by the birds that he saved himself from the black spirit of death: he was overcome at the hands of the fleet-footed descendant of Aeacus, in the river, just where he was ravaging the Trojans and others.
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ οὐκ … ἀλλ’ ἐδάμη is ‘but not … but was overcome’. οἰωνοῖσιν is a dative of means, ‘by birds’, that is by his reading of them. ἐρύσατο is the aorist middle of ἐρύομαι ‘draw to oneself, rescue’, so ‘draw off from himself’, with κῆρα μέλαιναν ‘the black death-fate’ as its object. ἐδάμη is the aorist passive of δαμάζω ‘subdue’, and ὑπὸ χερσί is ‘under the hands’. ποδώκεος Αἰακίδαο ‘of the fleet-footed descendant of Aeacus’ is Achilles, named by a patronymic (Aeacus was his grandfather). ἐν ποταμῷ ‘in the river’ is not named. κεράϊζε is the imperfect of κεραΐζω ‘ravage’, and its subject is the same Achilles, lying idle by the ships at the moment of the poem (2.772), so the death is told ahead of its time.

sentences.t:
Φόρκυς αὖ Φρύγας ἦγε καὶ Ἀσκάνιος θεοειδὴς
τῆλ’ ἐξ Ἀσκανίης·
sentences.l:
Phorcys, in turn, brought the Phrygians, and Ascanius, godlike in form,
far away, from Ascania;
sentences.i: Phorcys, in turn, and Ascanius, godlike in form, brought the Phrygians from far away, from Ascania;
sentences.n: Φόρκυς αὖ … ἦγε is ‘Phorcys, in turn, brought’, ἦγε being singular although Ἀσκάνιος follows, and Φρύγας is ‘Phrygians’. Ἀσκάνιος ‘Ascanius’ has θεοειδής ‘godlike in form’ (θεός + εἶδος ‘form’). τῆλ’ is τῆλε ‘far’, and ἐξ Ἀσκανίης ‘out of Ascania’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of 863.

sentences.t: μέμασαν δ’ ὑσμῖνι μάχεσθαι.
sentences.l: and they were eager in battle to fight.
sentences.i: and they were eager to fight in the battle.
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of 863. μέμασαν is a past form of μέμονα ‘be eager’, whose participle μεμαότες stood at 818: ‘they were eager’. ὑσμῖνι is the dative of ὑσμίνη ‘battle’, and μάχεσθαι ‘to fight’ is the infinitive that says what they were eager for. The subject, the Phrygians, is not named again.

sentences.t:
Μῄοσιν αὖ Μέσθλης τε καὶ Ἄντιφος ἡγησάσθην
υἷε Ταλαιμένεος τὼ Γυγαίη τέκε λίμνη,
οἳ καὶ Μῄονας ἦγον ὑπὸ Τμώλῳ γεγαῶτας.
sentences.l:
Over the Maeonians, in turn, Mesthles and Antiphus led,
the two sons of Talaemenes, whom the Gygaean lake bore,
who also brought the Maeonians born under Tmolus.
sentences.i: Over the Maeonians, in turn, Mesthles and Antiphus led, the two sons of Talaemenes, whom the Gygaean lake bore, who also brought the Maeonians born under Tmolus.
sentences.n: Μῄοσιν is the dative of Μῄονες ‘Maeonians’ (the same name as the accusative Μῄονας in the last line), here ‘over the Maeonians’, with ἡγησάσθην the dual aorist of ἡγέομαι ‘lead’ for the two men. Μέσθλης is ‘Mesthles’ and Ἄντιφος ‘Antiphus’, a name that also stood at 2.678 for a leader of the men of Cos. υἷε Ταλαιμένεος is ‘the two sons of Talaemenes’ (dual υἷε); τὼ is the dual relative ‘whom’, and Γυγαίη … λίμνη ‘the Gygaean lake’ is the subject of τέκε ‘bore’ (unaugmented), so the lake is their mother, in the poet’s phrase. οἳ καί ‘who also’ turns to the plural for the two; ἦγον is ‘brought’, and Μῄονας … γεγαῶτας is ‘the Maeonians born’, γεγαῶτας being the epic perfect participle of γίγνομαι, with ὑπὸ Τμώλῳ ‘under Tmolus’, a mountain.

sentences.t:
Νάστης αὖ Καρῶν ἡγήσατο βαρβαροφώνων,
οἳ Μίλητον ἔχον Φθιρῶν τ’ ὄρος ἀκριτόφυλλον
Μαιάνδρου τε ῥοὰς Μυκάλης τ’ αἰπεινὰ κάρηνα·
sentences.i: Nastes, in turn, led the Carians, who spoke a foreign tongue, who held Miletus and the mountain of the Phthires, thick with leaves, and the streams of the Maeander and the steep peaks of Mycale;
sentences.n: Νάστης is ‘Nastes’, αὖ ‘in turn’, and ἡγήσατο ‘led’ takes the genitive Καρῶν ‘the Carians’. βαρβαροφώνων ‘of barbarian speech’ (βάρβαρος + φωνή ‘voice’) names a people whose language a Greek could not follow, like the many tongues Iris spoke of at 804. οἳ … ἔχον is ‘who held’, with Μίλητον ‘Miletus’ and Φθιρῶν ὄρος ‘the mountain of the Phthires’, a name the Greek does not explain. ἀκριτόφυλλον ‘of unsorted leaves’ (ἄκριτος ‘unsorted’ + φύλλον ‘leaf’) is taken to mean thick with foliage. Μαιάνδρου … ῥοάς is ‘the streams of the Maeander’ (ῥοά ‘stream’), and Μυκάλης αἰπεινὰ κάρηνα ‘the steep peaks of Mycale’, κάρηνα, literally ‘heads’, being the peaks of a mountain and αἰπεινά a form of the adjective ‘steep’. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
τῶν μὲν ἄρ’ Ἀμφίμαχος καὶ Νάστης ἡγησάσθην,
Νάστης Ἀμφίμαχός τε Νομίονος ἀγλαὰ τέκνα,
sentences.l:
Of these, then, Amphimachus and Nastes led,
Nastes and Amphimachus, the splendid children of Nomion,
sentences.i: Of these, then, Amphimachus and Nastes led, Nastes and Amphimachus, Nomion’s splendid children,
sentences.n: τῶν μὲν ἄρ’ is ‘of these, then’, and ἡγησάσθην is the dual ‘led’, for two men. The pair is then said again in the other order, Νάστης Ἀμφίμαχός τε, with their father: Νομίονος is the genitive of Νομίων ‘Nomion’, and ἀγλαὰ τέκνα is ‘splendid children’, τέκνα (neuter) standing for the sons. The line is built like 2.620, which has an Amphimachus of another contingent; nothing here links the two.

sentences.t:
ὃς καὶ χρυσὸν ἔχων πόλεμον δ’ ἴεν ἠΰτε κούρη
νήπιος, οὐδέ τί οἱ τό γ’ ἐπήρκεσε λυγρὸν ὄλεθρον,
sentences.l:
who even with gold on him to war went like a girl,
foolish, and not at all for him did that ward off grievous destruction,
sentences.i: who even went to war with gold on him, like a girl, foolish as he was, and that did not at all ward off grievous destruction from him,
sentences.n: ὃς is singular, so it picks out one of the two; the nearer name is Ἀμφίμαχος, and he is taken to be the man. χρυσὸν ἔχων is ‘having gold’, that is wearing it; the Greek says nothing more of the gold here, and 875 shows Achilles taking it. πόλεμον δ’ ἴεν is ‘went to war’ (-δε of direction; ἴεν the imperfect of εἶμι), ἠΰτε κούρη ‘like a girl’, and νήπιος ‘foolish’ is the narrator’s comment on the man. οὐδέ τί οἱ is ‘and not at all for him’, τό γ’ ‘that at least’, the gold, and ἐπήρκεσε the aorist of ἐπαρκέω ‘ward off’, with the object λυγρὸν ὄλεθρον ‘grievous destruction’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἐδάμη ὑπὸ χερσὶ ποδώκεος Αἰακίδαο
ἐν ποταμῷ, χρυσὸν δ’ Ἀχιλεὺς ἐκόμισσε δαΐφρων.
sentences.l:
but he was subdued under the hands of the fleet-footed descendant of Aeacus
in the river, and the gold Achilles carried off, wise-minded.
sentences.i: but he was overcome at the hands of the fleet-footed descendant of Aeacus in the river, and wise-hearted Achilles carried off the gold.
sentences.n: The first line is the same as 860 and the second begins as 861, so the death is told in the same words: ‘subdued under the hands of the fleet-footed descendant of Aeacus, in the river’. Here Achilles is named, with Ἀχιλεύς (a single λ, the form the verse allows alongside Ἀχιλλεύς). ἐκόμισσε is the aorist of κομίζω, here ‘carry off’ as spoil, though the verb is elsewhere ‘take care of’. δαΐφρων ‘wise-minded’ is an old epithet whose first part is explained either from δαῆναι ‘to learn, know’ or from δαΐ ‘in battle’, so its sense is disputed.

sentences.t:
Σαρπηδὼν δ’ ἦρχεν Λυκίων καὶ Γλαῦκος ἀμύμων
τηλόθεν ἐκ Λυκίης, Ξάνθου ἄπο δινήεντος.
sentences.l:
And Sarpedon was leading the Lycians, and blameless Glaucus,
from far away, from Lycia, from the eddying Xanthus.
sentences.i: Sarpedon and blameless Glaucus led the Lycians, from far away, from Lycia, from the eddying Xanthus.
sentences.n: Σαρπηδὼν δ’ ἦρχεν Λυκίων is ‘and Sarpedon led the Lycians’, with ἦρχεν singular before the second name, Γλαῦκος ἀμύμων ‘blameless Glaucus’, ἀμύμων being the stock epithet whose real meaning is not known. τηλόθεν ἐκ Λυκίης is ‘from far away, from Lycia’, and Ξάνθου ἄπο δινήεντος ‘from the eddying Xanthus’ has ἄπο after its noun, with δινήεντος ‘eddying’ (δίνη ‘eddy’) as the river’s epithet. This is the last of the Trojan allies, and the last line of the book.
